General Perisic is represented today in this courtroom by the same Defence team, Novak Lukic, Gregor Guy-Smith, Dee Montgomery, Tina Drolec, Chad Mair and Boris Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I resume, Your Honours, I would like to make two interventions into the yesterday's transcript. We will have some minor interventions later on that we'll ask to be verified once we've checked the tape but this is what I would like to check. Page 14829, line 22 of the transcript. I don't know if that can be shown on our screens right now. If you recall, I spoke of the structure of the 30th Personnel Centre within the personnel administration at the time and I mentioned Generals Matovic and Zoric. [Interpretation] The next sentence: [In English] "He could tell Mladic and this is an administrative matter, quoting, 'I need a report about a situation with your family.'" [Interpretation] What I said was, for instance, could he have told Mladic so and so, and that's the way I'd like the transcript to be construed, and I think that's easy to deduce from the sentence before and after, that that was the parallel that I was drawing in my argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, at the very crucial stage of your intervention, there was an overlap and we don't know what you said because I heard a very loud voice in my ear. If you look at line 10 of page 2 you'll see that -- I beg your pardon, line 7, you said, "I spoke of the structure of the 30th Personnel Centre within the personnel administration at the time and I mentioned Generals Matovic and Zoric in this context I said English and then overlap." Can you repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was because I switched to English and that's why there was the overlap with the interpreter. What the transcript reads is on this page, page 14829, line 22 is [In English] "For instance, he could tell Mladic, and this is an administrative matter." [Interpretation] And then what follows is something that I have no issue with, but I'll say in English what it was that I said, [In English] "For instance, could he tell Mladic ..." [Interpretation] Could he have told Mladic, so that's the correction I'd like to make. And I have another correction to make. When on page 14834, I spoke of the Erak case. A moment, please. What reads in the transcript in English in line 21, when I spoke of his return -- my apologies, that's page 14834, the entire passage starts in line 24, but continues on the following page. And I said, this is what the transcript reads, [In English] "Quite the contrary, they prove voluntariness." [Interpretation] What I said in Serbian was that quite the contrary, this showed wilfulness. Thank the interpreters. I spoke of the wilfulness exhibited on the part of that individual. And let me go back, Your Honours, to where we left off yesterday. If you remember, in the latter part of my submissions, I spoke of the evidence which on the one hand show the commitment taken on the part of the leadership of the FRY and the VJ to peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, and on the other hand I used the same evidence to show examples of lack of control, absence of control, and the typical examples where attempts were made at exerting some sort of influence to bring these matters about. I will continue along the time-line that I followed and what comes next is the 40th session, which is P714 and I'll ask pages 2 and 3 in B/C/S and pages 2 and 3 in English to be shown. I'm going back to that story of the context that you need to bear in mind, the background, when we are talking about these issues. The session was held on the 5th of August, 1995, and I'll remind you that this was the time, a very traumatic time of the Croatian offensive against the RSK and the mass exodus that took place from Croatia. We don't have the transcript of the session, but we have the minutes which read as follows: "The president of Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the lower part of the page in English, "Contributing to the debate, president of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, noted that all the issues that had been raised were extremely difficult and that it was important to look at the situation in its entirety. He reminded everyone of the efforts invested by the FR Yugoslavia the previous year to get Republika Srpska to accept the Contact Group Plan and for the leadership of the RS Krajina to enter into dialogue with Zagreb. Unfortunately, from that moment on, a shift occurred between Knin and Pale. "And to the extent we were able to, we tried to bear upon the leadership of the RS Krajina to engage in dialogue with Zagreb." This is end of quote. I will move off to another example, another illustration which occurred only ten days later which was the 41st session of the Supreme Defence Council, P797. Because of the critical situation in view of Operation Storm which was on-going and the exodus of the Serb population from Krajina, this session was held -- was actually expanded, as you will see, including all of the senior officers of the VJ General Staff. It was in fact an expanded collegium of the VJ General Staff with SDC members. Page 24 in B/C/S, and 25 in English, is where Milosevic addressed all the generals who were present from the VJ General Staff and said: "Therefore, I kindly ask you as colleagues of these people to work upon them and use your influence as far as possible to make some -- to put some sense into them to make them realize it's absolutely impossible to wage a war against the whole world and the entire NATO pact and that there is no chance for any military success. Whoever has such half-crazy ideas must realise that the entire people would pay for it. Therefore we have to exert pressure and explain to them that the only settlement that can be found is through the peace plan. In this way we will resolve historical and existential issues and we will get rid of the war threat approaching the borders of Yugoslavia ." What followed next was the bombing of Republika Srpska. Therefore, the wish of the FRY leadership was to exert pressure, to work upon them with a view to putting a stop to the war. The background that I mentioned was the Croatian Muslim offensive in Bosnia, the Serb exodus from the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the Army of the RSK was practically non-existent at the time and on the other hand, the VRS officers had their salaries returned back in February and it was the members of the SDS and Perisic who met with Mladic on several occasions, this is what Mr. Harmon mentioned. And then we have another meeting of the SDS with General Mladic where he was invited to take part in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: SDC, the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, this was on the 23rd of August, 1995. Exhibit P713. Pages 5 and 6 in B/C/S and 5, 6, and 7 in English and that's the part that I would like to read fully. I am sorry, in English it's 5 and 6, and in B/C/S it's 5, 6, and 7. At the time of these discussions, there were talks held with Mr. Holbrooke and the international community with a view to finding a peace solution and the discussions were going on about who was going to represent the Serbs in these negotiations, and that's the subject of the debate here. Addressing General Mladic, President Milosevic repeated the possible options for stopping the war and resolving the crisis. Reiterating that we should strive and fight for peace. He therefore asked the general to make a public statement on behalf of the Army of Republika Srpska Main Staff consisting of one sentence, in inverted commas, "We accept peace. Matters would take a turn for the better for all the Serbs. And then guarantees could be obtained from authorised representatives of the international community for the Serbian population in the territories from which the Serbian army would withdraw. This would be supervised by the UN forces and be possibly even by NATO. The people would not have to leave their centuries-old homes." What follows next is a passage that is a bit more difficult to read. It reads: "General Mladic was asked to state" - what follows next is illegible - "whether he would accept a solution negotiated by President Milosevic." Again an illegible passage. "Fought for a peace and preserved Republika Srpska." The next sentence: "He did not wish to state his opinion, explaining his," I presume "view," but I won't speculate, "that he is 'only a soldier of the people and not an elected representative and has no such powers.' He would leave this to the politicians." The next sentence: "The reasoned arguments of," what I see here is, "Presidents Lilic and Bulatovic were of no help either." I don't know if the same names are transcribed in English. And another passage that follows next, "President Milosevic replied that in the interests of the Serbian people that he seemed to be -- to have so close to his heart, he would sign a statement testifying to his commitment to peace as for the benefit of all and guarantees -- and the way to save the Serbs from total destruction and to give guarantees to the negotiating team that everything agreed will be accepted and implemented." The text of the proposed public statement of General Mladic, commander of the Army of Republika Srpska Main Staff reads as follows: "I believe I'm acting in the best interest of the Serbian people and hereby state that on behalf of the Army of Republika Srpska Main Staff, I will accept the peace plan reached by President Milosevic in Geneva." What does the next line of the minutes read, let's see: "General Mladic refused to sign and then there's an illegible passage, leaving this for a meeting with politicians." Let us go back to the legal issues and findings that you should make on the basis of this evidence. What are the control mechanisms that according to the OTP General Perisic had at his disposal? According to the OTP, the fact that he received his salary from him, and not just Mladic, but the most significant part of the officers corps. He promotes them and verifies ranks to them and as the OTP says, they have mechanisms to order them to return to the Army of Yugoslavia and then, as the Prosecutor says, they have mechanisms to initiate disciplinary procedures, arrest, and even terminate their service. And in addition to Mladic's spectacular statements that without the FRY, the VRS would not be able to survive and that he purportedly feels to be a member of a single army, well, what do you conclude from this? This is simply a way to exert influence on Mladic. His reaction to that influence is that he does not wish to hear them out, he does not wish to hear what Perisic or Milosevic have to say, and the justification he draws upon is that he is merely a soldier of the people. The leadership and the military leadership of the FRY did not try to influence Mladic only. We have presented evidence about direct contacts with other senior officers of the VRS and the SVK. The first question that we put is why would one influence and persuade and besiege and beg someone who the Prosecution claims is, de jure, as a member of the Army of Yugoslavia, a subordinate to Perisic? I'm going to remind you of Exhibit D344 now. We dealt with that in our final brief as well. We dealt with this with witnesses and it was under seal at the time because of Mladic's diaries, but I would like us to look at it now within this context that I'm speaking of in open court. This is a meeting between General Perisic and his closest co-workers from the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and practically the entire Main Staff of the VRS and General Mladic on the 14th of August, 1994. That is to say, after the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia imposed sanctions on Republika Srpska after the decision was reached to stop the payment of salaries, the meeting took place in Crna Rijeka. Perisic, at the very outset, conveys the message of the state leadership of the FRY to them, the Main Staff, and the highest-ranking officers of the Army of Republika Srpska. And the message is that they are asking them not to obey the leadership of Republika Srpska. In Perisic's words, the leadership of Republika Srpska have doomed their own people to a catastrophe. Now, page 8 in English and page 8 in B/C/S, and in relation to those words, and those requests made by the state leadership of the FRY, it is what General Manojlo Milovanovic, Chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, is saying. He is uttering words that General Mladic is recording in his diary. And you will recall that during the trial, General Skrbic who was a witness confirmed those words to be authentic. This is what he says, Milovanovic: "You are asking us to reject the authority of our leadership. They were chosen by the people. They are as they are. I cannot refuse to obey such a leadership because you did not refuse to obey your leadership either." In a single sentence here, Your Honours, there is proof of General Milovanovic's position and that has shattered the entire theory of the Prosecution about the belonging of these officers to the VJ, about effective control, and even goes to show the inability to wield influence. These officers, who received their salaries from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, at that point in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia left them without any salaries. They regulated their status. They verified their ranks. It did not cross their minds to listen to Perisic's request and the request of the state leadership of the FRY and to go by it. In this episode, where were all of these means of control that the Prosecutor speaks of? The Prosecutor says that Perisic could have said to all of them then, Go back, all of you, I hereby issue an order for all of you to go back to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Otherwise that is what the state leadership of the FRY asked them to do. You know that that was the decision reached at that session. They all refused this request of the leadership of the FRY. We discussed this subject in quite a bit of detail in our final brief as well, so I'm not going to deal with it anymore at this point, but I would like to draw your attention to something that we wrote in our final brief. However, now I would like to talk about effective control and influence on the SVK. We wrote about that in our final brief in paragraphs 985 through 987, then 993, 994, 995, 1003 and 1156. The Prosecution, as we have heard at the beginning of Mr. Harmon's remarks, dropped the charges for not preventing the shelling of Zagreb. So the same mechanisms that are claimed to have been indicators of effective control, and those are, as I mentioned a moment ago, all of that being insufficient salaries, decisions on appointment, administrative orders, verifications. All of that, all of these mechanisms of effective control obviously were totally insufficient for establishing any kind of effective control on the part of General Perisic in terms of preventing the shelling of Zagreb. All of these arguments were refuted by one single influence that could not function in military structures anymore, it certainly could not get close to the level of an order or effective control. Could we please move into private session for a movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like us to have a look at a brief section of an intercepted conversation between Milosevic and General Perisic on the 2nd of May, 1995, P1314. We note that that is the day when the first shelling of the city of Zagreb took place. "Milosevic: Did you say that that should not be done? "Perisic: I told them not to do it anymore. He says, 'Listen, I have to defend myself, I have no choice, you are not helping me, I have to defend myself.' "Milosevic: He is crazy."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just wait until we get to the next page. Okay. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then General Perisic says: "Perisic: I can tell you. "Milosevic: Now they are taking care of the cease-fire, he is bombing Zagreb." Another Exhibit P1297. In that document it say that is this intercepted conversation was taking place on the same day at 11.35 a.m., the same two interlocutors. "Milosevic: How dare they do that. "Perisic: Well, how. You can see that all of them are crazy, Mr. President. "Milosevic: The peace talks are continuing at 3.00 and all of that, but are they doing all of this on purpose?" I'm going to provide a comment at this point, let me give you the context. At 3.00 p.m., talks are supposed to continue between the premier of Republika Srpska Krajina, Mikelic, with the Croatian government about the cessation of hostilities in Western Slavonia. And now Perisic goes on to say: "They are not in line with each other. This Martic, I have a feeling that he is lost and that he doesn't think about the situation at all. "Milosevic: Did you tell Celeketic that this must not be done? "Perisic: Well, I did tell Celeketic, but it seems that he and Martic did it without our knowledge. They shelled Karlovac, Sisak, and now, as you see, also Zagreb." Can we now move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I conclude in relation to influence and control, the evidence that was adduced during these proceedings do not show that General Perisic had any mechanism of authority that goes beyond the level of influence, and also that this influence over his alleged subordinates sometimes had limited success, sometimes had some success, and sometimes failed altogether. It all depended on whether those whom the Prosecution identifies as his subordinates, perpetrators of crimes, wanted – and I underscore the word wanted – to accept his requests. However, he did not have any mechanisms in view of these requests made to these persons to make them perceive these requests as orders, naredjenje or naredba. This was not because they did not understand that from a military point of view they could suffer any consequences, because they knew that they were not in the chain of command of the VJ. As I've already mentioned on a number of occasions, the relationship that actually had a bearing on influence, and not on control, is a strong argument showing that there was a lack or that there was no control. Now, I will move on to another topic that has to do with certain indicia of effective control that the Prosecutor is using as -- and claiming that they were mechanisms that General Perisic had at his disposal to discipline. The Prosecutor claims that General Perisic had the mechanisms to discipline his subordinates in the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres and that that was evidence of effective control. The Prosecutor is also trying to show that he did use those mechanisms, but selectively and not when they related to war crimes. At the outset, I would like to stress one more time something that I said yesterday regarding the legal test, the legal standard of the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal is that the lack of power of a commander to prevent or punish must be met at the time of the commission of the crime. We claim that General Perisic did not have that power at the time of the crimes with which he is charged as the superior officer, nor later on, because the individuals that are identified as perpetrators, as his subordinates never entered, not even later, the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia because they were never assigned to any duty in any unit of the Army of Yugoslavia. His ability to use this mechanism, the Prosecutor finds in his de jure authority, which is envisaged pursuant to the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, and then he goes on to cite the law itself, which is P197. Now, we would like to stress that the same law, in its Article 181, paragraph 1 that I mentioned yesterday, is very clear. It clearly makes a distinction between the authority to initiate disciplinary proceedings against individuals who are members of the army and those outside of it. Specifically, all persons who are outside of the Army of Yugoslavia, for instance, the staff of the Ministry of Defence, the exclusive authority to take disciplinary action against those people is in the hands of the minister of defence. There's absolutely no authority at the General Staff, or the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army to initiate disciplinary proceedings over such individuals who are outside of the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia. Perisic did use his legal authority over those individuals who were within the Army of Yugoslavia, so the proceedings that were initiated against Boro Ivanovic, General Boro Ivanovic were done in keeping with that. He was a general within the Yugoslav Army, Perisic used all his legal power, initiating disciplinary proceedings against him and we saw what the outcome was. Mr. Guy-Smith mentioned this, at the27th session of the Supreme Defence Council, criticised him and said that he should seize all the proceedings and at the 29th session, the proceedings were quashed, against General Perisic's will. This was done by -- pursuant to a decision of the members of the Supreme Defence Council and, as I mentioned yesterday, and you have it all in evidence, at the 30th session, they actually promoted this general against the will of General Perisic. Therefore, that was where General Perisic used his legal authority to discipline persons who were serving within the Army of Yugoslavia. Now, the case of Colonel Babic that the Prosecutor cited as an example that there was a mechanism at the disposal of General Perisic to move for disciplinary proceedings are consistent with this case, and that is our reading of this document. Now, if you look at D2414, and that is the document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: P2414.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the document that the Prosecutor used to show that Perisic did have the authority to launch disciplinary proceedings. This document, dated December 1995, shows that Colonel Laza Babic at that point in time served at the Military Post 1122 in Belgrade. In other words, he was assigned to a post within the Army of Yugoslavia at that point in time unlike other members of the 40th Personnel Centre which were not assigned to any post, and therefore in this case, General Perisic used his authority in terms of this individual, who returned to the Army of Yugoslavia and was assigned to a post within the Army of Yugoslavia to take -- to discipline this individual if that was needed. This was the same case, the same case applied. This is totally different to the case of Bulat. The case of Bulat and other officers within the 40th Personnel Centre is in the following: None of them were assigned to the post in the Army of Yugoslavia. Once they are outside the command chain of the Army of Yugoslavia, Perisic did not have any legal authority to initiate any proceedings against them. This is why the decision in his case was made by the Supreme Defence Council, which was a superior organ to Perisic and the only organ that was superior to him, and that could command the Army of Yugoslavia, pursuant to orders of the President of Yugoslavia and once they issue an order which does not constitute a crime General Perisic has to implement that under the law. The Prosecutor cited the words of General Perisic at a collegium of the Chief of the General Staff on the 6th of November, 1995. You remember the words, "I can arrest him but I won't." That was P2204. But if we put this chronologically in context and see what it was that led Perisic to say those words in the collegium session, I would refer you to P703 to check that. That is the session of the Supreme Defence Council, the 43rd session, the BH page should be page 2, and English page 1, this was on the 30th of August, 1995, in other words two months preceding the words said by Perisic at that other session. My apologies, P708. Document P708. And I would like to point you to conclusion number 2. We see that this is a document from August 1995, and please bear that in mind when you assess the evidence shown by the Prosecutor. This was a conclusion taken on the 29th of August, 1995. Could we have the next page in B/C/S. We need paragraph 2, where it says: "Disciplinary or criminal proceedings shall be initiated against professional members of the 40th Personnel Centre for whom there are grounds to believe that they have committed a violation of discipline or a criminal offence." At the next session of the Supreme Defence Council, P765, which was held on the 6th of September of the same year, we can again take a look at the conclusions, that is on page 2 in English and page 2 in B/C/S. Because in this order coming from this session, they are discussing the need to specify, to give more precise explanation and supplement paragraph 4 of the earlier session and the initiation of those proceedings now sounds as follows, in place of the earlier point 4, and then it says what it sounded like, the following text was adopted: "Officers and non-commissioned officers who are found to have aced in a professional and dignified manner and bear no responsibility for the events in the RSK which unfolded between the 4th and 14th of August, 1995, may selectively be assigned to appropriate units and institutions of the Yugoslav Army or to the 30th Personnel Centre." That was a conclusion taken by the Supreme Defence Council which General Perisic had to implement and also there is a point made there that they were not at that point in time members of the Yugoslav Army but they should be assigned to it. In other words, the Supreme Defence Council adopts a conclusion that is binding on General Perisic in terms of those individuals who at that point in time are not within the Army of Yugoslavia but are to be assigned to posts in various units. And there, as we can see, the only thing that is discussed is the crimes that they had committed if they had committed them between the 4th and 14th of August, 1995. And that is what this decision of the Supreme Defence Council refers to. This was the case of Colonel Bulat. He was not assigned to any post or any duty in the Army of Yugoslavia. There were certain crimes that are discussed here that had to do with his surrender of his corps and that is what this relates to, for the period of time as mentioned. Now, you have to bear another thing in mind. At that time between August and November, December, the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina no longer existed. The military courts no longer existed, nor any military disciplinary courts in the Krajina, unlike the Serbian system where --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Unlike the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where both the military, judiciary and the military functioned throughout the end of the war. So let me conclude on this topic. In terms of the individuals that the Prosecutor said were his subordinates, General Perisic did not have the mechanisms to take disciplinary measures which he had under the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia. The cases that the Prosecutor has shown here had to do exclusively with those matters where he took action pursuant to orders from the Supreme Defence Council of Yugoslavia. I will add one more thing, and that has to do with command responsibility. I will discuss briefly the mechanisms of preventing crimes from being committed. The Prosecutor claims that General Perisic had the mechanisms to prevent the alleged subordinates from committing the crimes because he could order them to return to the Army of Yugoslavia. Paragraph 786. Now, please take a look at this paragraph. In this paragraph again, the Prosecutor actually highlights and supports our thesis that those individuals not in the Army of Yugoslavia. But let us see whether General Perisic had any mechanisms to issue any orders to the members of the 30th or 40th Personnel Centre to return or to be returned to the Army of Yugoslavia. In the absence of evidence to support this thesis, the Prosecutor refers to evidence which he misinterprets and also misquotes in addition to that. The Prosecutor speaking of the mechanism of effective control where he discusses the transfers and appointments, in paragraph 785 of his brief, the Prosecutor says the following, and I will read this out in English: [In English] "Perisic's authority to transfer and appointment VJ members to the VRS and SVK, and his exercise of it was indispensable life-line that sustained the vitality and viability of VRS and SVK. As Mladic informed Milosevic, quoting, 'the assistance of FRY," and then three full stops, "the army was invaluable. It will be difficult to imagine a course of events if it had not been for that assistance. It was comprehensive.'" Sorry. Now, when the Prosecutors quoted in this paragraph the words of General Mladic quoting this sentence, it quoted Exhibit P2710. Now, let us take a look at this exhibit and see what it really says. Can we have P2710 on the screens, please. This is General Mladic's letter addressed to President Milosevic on the 17th of December, 1995, after the signing of the Dayton Accords. And the sentence that was quoted by the Prosecution in its final brief as I read it out a little earlier, we can see it here, a reference to it here at the very beginning. "Mr. President, all this time of war, the assistance of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and especially Serbia and your own personally to Republika Srpska and the army was invaluable. It would be difficult to imagine the course of events if it had not been for that assistance. It was comprehensive, and basically, timely." Now, if you read out the entire document, and I know that you will do it with due care, there is no mention whatsoever here of the Army of Yugoslavia, the army that is mentioned is the Army of Republika Srpska and yet we have the words and the quotations as used by the Prosecutor in the final brief and you can judge it for yourself where he is referring to this document as being a reference to the Army of Yugoslavia. Now, I would like you to put this in the same context that Mr. Guy-Smith mentioned two days ago when he discussed the importance of the treatment of the context. So please bear this example in mind as well. But let us now go back to the main topic. This is something that the OTP submitted and has to do with this exhibit. Now, the topic is, could General Perisic have orders for the members of the Army of Yugoslavia as they put it and as we put it, members of the VRS to be taken back to the VJ ranks and to be -- to issue orders to that effect and that should prove the control mechanism. And what we are dealing here is with food and flour. Nowhere in the document is there any mention of any army. It is only the necessities and needs on the part of Republika Srpska that are mentioned here. The OTP have put forth an entire body of evidence -- or actually, have ignored an entire body of evidence about the procedures and authorities to bring about the return of personnel to the VJ, and this is something that I mentioned yesterday. An officer who wanted to return to the Army of Yugoslavia could have done so only with the approval and consent of his superior officers within the VRS, and General Perisic could not issue any orders in that context whatsoever. The evidence that the Prosecution relies upon in support of this thesis are documents about a procedure which was set up and that was operational, but these were final orders, naredba, which were as virtual as the orders that we referred to yesterday, the orders on transfer, which were important to have their status regulated. But they always stemmed from the procedure itself, which was that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and that's what we are interested most in here, when we are talking about the provision of the officers corps and control mechanism, as well as the army of the SRK. I think that they were invoking the document involving Babic and Republika Srpska. They were taken out of context. I don't have the paragraph here at hand, but this was something that the Prosecution relies upon in supporting their thesis of the control mechanism, and they had to do with the documentation relating to Officer Babic, but taken in isolation, they cannot lead to a reasonable finding that there was anything that could be done on the part of the Army of Yugoslavia. And this is something that should be viewed together with Article 33 of the instructions governing the work of personnel centres that were mentioned yesterday, as well as the testimony given by witnesses who were involved in this process. We had two witnesses to that effect and both Skrbic and Malcic testified to the mechanism as it was and which had to work solely with the consent of the Main Staff. And Skrbic referred to the very rigid position by General Mladic as to who would be allowed to return to the Army of Yugoslavia. All those who left the VRS ranks without that consent, without that approval, were regarded as deserters, and that was the case of Antic and Vujic, if you recall. I will not be discussing this evidence because you have seen the submissions on the part of the Prosecution, we've given you our submissions in our final trial brief. I cannot add to anything more than that. Can we move into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the other hand when we are discussing the orders and transfers which I continue submitting were virtual, and I explained to you yesterday why I am of this view, there is another example, a fact that I would like to remind you of. This is the testimony of a witness who himself experienced one such administrative order and described his response to it. General Novakovic testified that he had refused the decree issued by President Lilic in 1991, appointing him to a position within the VJ, that of the assistant Chief of General Staff for ground forces. When we showed him this entry in his personnel file, an entry that does exist in his personnel file, he simply said, at page 13278, he said that he had told President Lilic that he would not accept that appointment. And what happened? Nothing. Is that an example of subordination? What sort of -- which argument in this part of testimony, which was not challenged by the Prosecution in that portion, would the Prosecution offer of an officer saying no to his purported superior – President Lilic being precisely that in relation to General Novakovic - and bearing no consequences for it and then what, the superior would say, very well, I will not be asking anything more of you. Sorry. Would that be what they would say? So, when it was asked by the SDC that members of the 40th Personnel Centre, after the fall of the RSK, should report to the 30th Personnel Centre, this was P798 and P766, witness Novakovic, General Novakovic at the time, was asked to do so, he refused. And this was found interesting by the presiding judge and asked for an additional answer as to whether there were any consequences borne by him because there was the constant transfer of personnel. He answered, at page 13349, that he bore no consequences whatever in relation to that. So what sort of a finding can you make on the basis of evidence? Well, most certainly you cannot conclude that Perisic was able to order anyone to return to the VJ. Nor that any of the senior officers, and I mean the senior officers from the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres, were aware of the fact that they could do so themselves, that's to say, return to the ranks of the VJ without having obtained prior approval from their superiors within the VRS. They knew that if they took such steps that they would be liable to disciplinary procedures within their armies. That's to say, VRS and the SVK. Let me make my final findings concerning command responsibility. The Prosecution did not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that any of the elements of this responsibility were present and that primarily there existed the superior-subordinate relationship that I referred to yesterday, the other elements we dealt with in our final brief. There was no superior-subordinate relationship between General Perisic and those that the Prosecution indicated as perpetrators of crimes and as his subordinates. Another point that I would like to make before I move to my final thesis, and that's P2879, and that's the video-clip of an interview, I think it was the vice-president of Republic of Serbia at the time, General Perisic, this was sometime in 2000. You saw him in civilian clothing there. But you have to review the entire clip. It covered the latter period of the dissolution of the SFRY and JNA. It covered this long period of disintegration from the start of the conflict to the end of the conflict in Kosovo, I believe. This is an edited TV show with many participants who spoke of various topics and events. They talk without having any questions put to them. There is no proper course of the conversation. You could actually fall into a trap of arriving at conclusions that could be highly unreliable. We cannot conclude on the basis of this interview as to what specifically General Perisic was asked about and what period he was discussing. This sort of evidence should be dealt with carefully because their probative value is highly limited. I would like to move on to my final stage of submission, so perhaps we should take our break a bit earlier. I will not take much more time.

This document that you say we must --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Harmon made a mistake in the number of the document. That's where the confusion perhaps arose from. It's a transcription of the TV show.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, let's get things clear. The transcript is P2879. What is this transcript's exhibit number? I see Mr. Harmon on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could be of assistance.
