utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we heard many submissions from the Prosecution about Perisic's alleged support of the war and especially about his actions which contributed to the crimes themselves. We assert that this is not true and that this has not been proven. It is not a crime to assist in waging a war, and this is something that Mr. Guy-Smith referred to in his submissions, however horrible a thing war itself is. General Perisic headed the VJ General Staff in the most difficult years in the time of crisis in the former Yugoslavia, when the FRY was isolated under sanctions and exposed to constant attempts to be drawn into the war by alleged friend and foe. Under the constitution and in law, Perisic had the task of protecting the security and territorial integrity of the country and he did carry out his professional obligation. To the regret of many, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was not drawn into the war, nor did the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia participate in the war at the time he was the Chief of the General Staff. Certain elements of the Special Units Corps did take part in Operation Pancir 2 in the area of Sarajevo in December and January, that's to say, December 1993 and January 1994, but this was an isolated case and in our submission the presence of the unit in Vogosca did not have anything to do with the crimes which were committed at the time and there is nothing to prove that they did have to do anything with them. The Prosecution ignores many actions taken by General Perisic during and after the war and which were directly related to the wish that peace be established, further human victims be avoided, and new conflicts be prevented from emerging. You cannot ignore it. I will mention only several events and certain evidence indicating what it was and how General Perisic worked. Perisic should take most of the credit for the fact that around 1.000 Muslims and their troops who had swam across the Drina River fleeing Zepa on the 1st and 2nd August, 1995, finding refuge in the FRY, for receiving those, some of whom expressed a wish to move on to other countries and ones who remained as refugees within the FRY. Whatever the attempts to ignore this or to misinterpret the fact that Perisic did everything in respect of these people who sought refuge in the FRY to keep them within the FRY rather than have them return to the place they fled. Look at testimony by Witness Borovic at transcript page 14003 and this, among other things, was the trigger that prompted Milosevic to send a letter to both Mladic and Alija Izetbegovic to ask them to stop the war and the trigger was in fact this incident where people swam across the Drina River and this is in Exhibit D490 and 489. As for Perisic's role in the liberation of the French pilots and liberation of the French hostages, Medecins Sans Frontieres, you heard a great deal about it. You heard the Prosecution's interpretation of the evidence as well as the Defence's. I will not add to this further since Mr. Guy-Smith spoke of the significance that the freeing of the French pilots had internationally. When we spoke of influence and control in our final brief, we explained to what direction his actions tended when he dealt with General Mladic and what sort of role this had in the war itself. General Clark -- and this is what expert Treanor mentioned in his expert report P375 paragraph 240 where he said that at the meeting with Tudjman and Holbrooke, Clark said that Perisic in his view had -- was unable to exert influence over Mladic. Perisic, throughout his tenure at the head of the General Staff, was afraid of the reactions the conflicts might have in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia and the bearing it might have on the stability of the FRY. To gain an insight into this, you can look to many minutes of the SDC meetings where Perisic spoke of the various problems, of the potential for the conflict to spill over into the FRY, and of the problem which arose at the time which was that of Kosovo. Unfortunately, his foreboding proved true, the war in Kosovo occurred in 1999, and you also heard evidence to the effect of his role in fighting for -- in asking that the war be averted. He didn't want the war in Kosovo. He feared it and saw it coming. That's why he signed the agreement with General Clark. This is D752, about agreeing to the arrival of international observers in Kosovo. He was still the Chief of the General Staff. He did this because he knew what might happen if the entire international community turned against them. A moment ago I read out Milosevic's words from a meeting in 1995 about his fears as to what would become of Bosnia-Herzegovina if the entire international community turned against it and why was it that Milosevic -- that these words slipped his mind when he was contemplating the war in Kosovo. Because of this attitude of his towards the participation of the army and the war in Kosovo and avoiding the spread of conflict, Milosevic, under quotation marks, rewarded Perisic by dismissing him and even initiating criminal proceedings against him. Demoting him altogether. I would like to refer to an episode that occurred while Perisic was still Chief of General Staff and this was the focus of attention. We saw how many times he clashed with Milosevic. We saw the episode with General Boro Ivanovic, and this is directly linked to the evidence. However, there was something that happened in public for the first time, he took a position in relation to Milosevic's policy. General Perisic expressed that in 1997 during the so-called student protests. Perhaps I am a bit partial when I say this, and a Defence attorney should not be partial, we have adduced evidence showing that General Perisic did not allow the army to interfere in any way in that conflict between Milosevic and those who were protesting and both the students and the opposition and the democratic public in the FRY and worldwide supported that. As for Milosevic, he distanced himself from him very clearly in public. This move was supported by the students who were protesting, of course, the democratic opposition in Serbia, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time. I think that by then it was the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro. It was the first time that this came to the fore, this relationship between Milosevic and Perisic, and the international community recognised that. We wrote about that in our final brief and we see all these moves that he took, and we are closing the circle by saying that when General Perisic was a member of the federal parliament of Serbia and Montenegro, he voted in favour of changing laws and regulations concerning co-operation with The Hague Tribunal, making it possible to have citizens of the country sent to The Hague Tribunal, those who were suspects and who were indicted. Mr. Perisic was the only one who then knew that he might be here before you, but he nevertheless voted in favour of that law and in having his fate put into your hands. Then, in his public statement concerning his voluntary surrender, he said that there was no dilemma in his mind as to whether he would appear before this Tribunal, because he said that that was the only way in which he would defend his honour, the reputation of the army, and the dignity of the people. In his introductory remarks when this trial started, he stated that he was confident that without prejudice, professionally and carefully you will reach an honourable and fair judgement. Your Honours, you are to assess these words of his. Without prejudice that, and all of us who interpret the facts and events are full of prejudice. This should be done professionally and in the spirit of what the international community has entrusted you with, accepted standards in assessing innocence or responsibility. This is the priority of your task. Only after a judgement is reached in this way, can the international community face the other part of the mandate that was given to this Tribunal, justice for the victims and the return of trust among the peoples in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. That has to be the order taken, the sequence of events that should follow. First, the truth should be established, facts beyond a reasonable doubt. I am going to use a social, a societal term, it is the truth that has to be your priority because on the basis of the truth, there can be justice for the victims and it is only through justice for the victims that there can be reconciliation for the peoples of the former Yugoslavia. If you establish the truth and if you free all of us of prejudice, all of us from the former Yugoslavia, then you would have accomplished your mission. We believe that General Perisic defended his honour before this court, the reputation of the army, and the dignity of the people. That is why we ask that he be acquitted of all charges in all counts of the indictment. Thank you for having given us this opportunity of making our closing arguments. Thank you. I'm prepared to answer any questions you may have now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Harmon, any rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have a few submissions. It won't take long but we need the podium moved from the Defence side. Thank you. And the way we will proceed, Your Honours, is Ms. McKenna will make submissions first, Mr. Thomas will go next, and I will conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam McKenna, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'll be making two brief submissions in rebuttal. Firstly, the Defence conflates the basis for Article 7(1) liability and Article 7(3) liability. The issue of whether a superior-subordinate relationship existing between Perisic and the members of the personnel centres is relevant only to a Article 7(3) analysis. Equally, the issue of whether personnel centre members were part of the VJ chain of command has no relevance to an assessment of Perisic's liability under Article 7(1). The Defence conflates these issues. Throughout Mr. Lukic's submission on Perisic's liability under Article 7(1) for the provision of personnel, he discussed whether the personnel centre members remained within the VJ chain of command. So for example, at T-14802, line 1 and onwards, with reference to the officers transferred to the VRS, he stated that "from that moment onwards, they became part of that single chain of command. They had their own oath and they had their own superiors. They were part of a functioning army within their chain of command established by law." He then went on to undertake a detailed review of VRS documents relating to the appointment of certain officers to particular posts within the VRS, in support of the Defence proposition that those officers were solely within the chain of command of the VRS. And I will return to this issue of appointment in my second submission. But under Article 7(1), the relevant issue is whether Perisic provided assistance which had a substantial effect on the crimes committed. In the Prosecution's submission, this assistance included personnel, the provision of personnel through the personnel centres. However, an inquiry into whether the chain of command between Perisic and members of the personnel centres was broken when they were serving in the VRS, whether they were under a dual chain of command while they were serving there, or whether Perisic continued to be their superior while they were in Bosnia-Herzegovina is relevant only to an examination of Perisic's liability under Article 7(3). In the Prosecution's submission, by maintaining and sustaining the VRS officer corps through the personnel centres, including by ensuring that the officers' status rights will be fully protected and enjoyed while they were serving outside the FRY by the effective regulation of those officers' service, thereby assuring the officers of their livelihood and assuring the VRS command of a solid command structure, Perisic's acts had a substantial effect on the crimes alleged. Turning to my very brief second submission, and this relates to appointments. The Defence stated with reference to the Prosecution brief and the Prosecution closing arguments, that it was the Prosecution claim that Perisic had the authority to appoint within the VRS itself. And that's at T-14831, line 23 and following. The Defence misunderstands the Prosecution position. As stated in the Prosecution's closing arguments, at lines T-14698 and following, the Prosecution does not dispute that the VRS and the SVK made the majority of decisions as to assignment to duty within those armies, and that the duties to which those officers were assigned in the personnel centres reflected the decisions that had been made by the VRS and the SVK commands. And if I may move very briefly into closed session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Closed or private?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Sorry, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The paragraph of the Prosecution brief, paragraph 183 to which the Defence referred in its submission, reads: "Having transferred VJ officers to the personnel centres, the VJ also regulated internal appointments to different units within the VRS and the SVK ensuring the effective functioning of the personnel centre system." Your Honours, for the avoidance of any confusion, the Prosecution does not suggest that Perisic made appointments within the VRS or the SVK. Rather it is the Prosecution's submission that while the VRS and the SVK made determinations as to appointments to particular duties within those armies, in accordance with their needs of service, Perisic and the VJ had the ultimate authority as to whether an individual returned to the FRY. And contrary to Mr. Lukic's suggestion this morning, this was discussed -- this issue was discussed in the Prosecution's closing submissions on Monday and is also discussed in the final brief, in the Prosecution's brief at paragraphs 190 to 193. Your Honours, unless you have any further questions, that concludes my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to discuss briefly, Your Honours, a point made by my learned friend Mr. Lukic yesterday, elements of which have emerged again in his submissions to you this morning. A position that he took yesterday was that under the VJ law, under the law of the army, personnel transferred to the VRS or the SVK did not come under the responsibility of the VJ any longer, as they had been assigned outside of the VJ and that therefore as a result, Perisic did not have any obligation to discipline them if the need arose or to otherwise carry out the duties of a superior. The position adopted by the Defence was that in respect of such individuals assigned outside of the VJ, that if anyone besides the army's concerned, that is, the VRS and SVK had that responsibility, it was the Ministry of Defence. That position misunderstands the Law of the VJ and it misunderstands the evidence relating to it. And what I would like to do, Your Honours, is to go through the parts, the transcript references and state the Prosecution's position in relation to each of the propositions made by my learned friend and once I've done that, I will take Your Honours to the relevant legal provisions. But before I do, Your Honours, as a -- as a brief introductory point, it is trite after all of the evidence that we have heard that the Law of the VJ did not contemplate the sending of VJ officers to another army. It does not provide for that. It simply does not contemplate it. Those are what the provisions of the Law on the VJ state, and the evidence in relation to those provisions, Your Honours, is discussed in paragraph 172 of the Prosecution's final trial brief. What the Law on the VJ did permit was for the Chief of the General Staff to make assignments of VJ officers to units or organisations outside of the VJ, including the Ministry of Defence, but not limited to the Ministry of Defence. The Law of the VJ, as I said, did not extend to sending officers to another army. General Perisic knew that, that's what he told the SDC when advocating for the formation of the personnel centres themselves. It was because of the complete absence of any legal basis to send officers to these armies that we have the personnel centres being advocated for in the first place. The benefits of those centres have been described in various ways, but one of the reasons for their genesis lay in the absence of any legal basis for what the FRY, the SDC, General Perisic were proposing and what they had been doing up until that point when he became Chief of the General Staff of the VJ. So if I move -- before I move, Your Honours, to the transcripts, having created the personnel centres, the difficulty arose as to how to legally categorise and classify these particular individuals for, amongst other thing, the application of the law. How was the Law on the VJ to apply to these officers. How were the regulations and laws relating to the regulation of status, promotion, other service rights, all things that that apply to all servicemen supposed to apply to these people who now had been transferred out of the FRY into Bosnia or Croatia, in contravention of the law or in the absence of any express provision regulating that in the Law of the VJ. The response of the courts, the response of the VJ itself was to categorise these individuals as VJ members who had been assigned outside of the army. That is the language used throughout the military court decisions. That is the language described throughout the military court decisions that we have seen tendered in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, do you have a glass of water in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Actually something else, Your Honours, may I just have a moment. The language used in the decisions of the supreme military courts and other decisions is that these persons were governed by the laws relating to VJ servicemen, because they were to be considered members of the VJ who had been assigned outside the army of the VJ, who had been assigned outside the VJ. And that is a term of art. It is a legal term of art that is drawn from the Law of the VJ itself. It is language that is also used by General Nikolic, the systems and status related issues chief from the FRY MOD when he testified, and this was a position that the VJ itself before those military courts never challenged. It was agreed and all of those proceedings resulting in all of the judgements that Your Honours have been provided with during the course of this trial, it was agreed by the VJ that these officers were VJ members serving outside the VJ, that that is the status that they enjoyed in terms of being able to classify them under the Law of the VJ. I'd like to directly answer individual propositions made by my learned friend before going to those provisions, Your Honour, and Mr. Registrar, if it is possible, I wonder if we could have yesterday's transcript, T-14811, at line 25 on the screen. Now, Your Honours, if you go to line -- if we can go to line 25, right. Mr. Lukic says at that point: "Even if they had been," and we are talking about the officers in the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres, "even if they had been members of the VJ serving outside the VJ, they were no longer part of their chain of command. The army of -- the Law of the Army of Yugoslavia which is Exhibit 197, stipulates that precisely ..." Let me be very clear. It does not stipulate that. On the next page at line 7: "The Law on the Army of Yugoslavia is quite precise in respect of the status and rights and obligations of those serving outside the VJ." Yes, we are agreed. It is, in respect of the rights and obligations of those termed as serving outside the VJ. "They were definitely outside the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia under Article 8(2) of the law." No, that is incorrect, Your Honours. The only people who could possibly fall into that category, because they were expressly provided for in this respect, were VJ officers assigned to the Ministry of Defence. "Those outside -- sorry, "Those serving outside the VJ," the next line, "they had the same rights and obligations as if they were members of the army unless provided otherwise by the law." Well, there was no provision otherwise in respect of people serving in the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres, and yes, we agree that they had the same rights and obligations as if they were members of the army. If we move to page 812, line 20, please. It's there on the screen. My learned friend said: "The Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, Your Honours, has to do with the commanding officers serving outside the VJ, regulating their status in relation to their promotion, appointment to duty, transfer, and termination of service ..." Yes, up to that point we agree with that submission. "... defining that these aspects lay solely with the Ministry of Defence." Absolutely not. It lay with the Ministry of Defence only in respect of servicemen assigned specifically to the Ministry of Defence. "The Army of Yugoslavia" -- sorry, the next line down, Your Honours, "The Army of Yugoslavia has no input including the General Staff and its chief." In relation to those assigned to the MOD, that is correct. In respect of everybody else, that is mistaken. Page 813, line 5: "If a VJ officer is serving outside the VJ, all of the aspects of his service were exclusively in the remit of those who were in charge of the armies where they served, not the VJ. That is stipulated by the law." Well, obviously Mr. Lukic couldn't cite to any such provision. It doesn't exist in the Law of the VJ, which does not contemplate anything of the sort. Page 813, line 11: "The Army of Yugoslavia is competent to initiate disciplinary procedure only vis-a-vis those people who are within the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia." Yes, agreed, but the position that Mr. Lukic has miscalculated is that those who are assigned, VJ members who are assigned outside of the VJ including the 30th and 40th as they were treated, still fall within this category under law. Disciplinary responsibility is retained by the VJ and I will demonstrate that in a moment, Your Honours. "In respect of the individuals who are outside the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia, for instance, the law refers to the Ministry of Defence, Article 181 confers the sole responsibility for the initiation of a disciplinary procedure upon the Ministry of Defence." Only, only, Your Honours, in respect of VJ servicemen assigned to the MOD. In respect of everybody else, that disciplinary responsibility is retained by the army. So, let me take you to just several of these provisions which can illustrate that for you. If we could have P197 on the screen, please, Mr. Registrar. I'm looking, please, first of all for Article 8, which is on page 3 of the English and page 2 in the B/C/S. Page 3 in the English, sorry, Mr. Registrar. Your Honour, this article, Article 8, is the provision which states for us that service in the VJ includes service outside of the VJ. It's referred to in the second paragraph of Article 8 which reads: "Service in the army shall also include military and other duties in the Federal Ministry of Defence, other state organ, company or other organisation performed by professional members of the army assigned there by an order of an authorised officer (hereinafter assignments outside the army)." Service in the army shall include assignments outside the army. Now, as I've said, there's no express inclusion of transfer to another army, which of course, is not contemplated for a moment by this law. But for the purposes of this law, the VJ and the courts, as I've already identified, treated 30th and 40th Personnel Centre officers as officers assigned outside the army or serving outside the army. Under Article 8, that is service in the VJ. So we begin there. If we could go to Article 152, please. And, Mr. Registrar, that is on page 38 of the English and page 13 of the B/C/S. Now, Article 152, Your Honours, regulates the number of tasks or responsibilities of the Chief of the General Staff and commanding units, promotion, appointments and so on, matters relating to the service of an individual. But paragraph 5 states that the Chief of the General Staff shall "decide on the assignment of professional members of the army to duties outside the army, while assignment to the Federal Ministry of Defence shall be carried out at the request or with the approval of the Federal Minister of Defence, or a commanding officer authorised by him." So we have for the first time the special category created of an assignment to the Federal Ministry of Defence as opposed to an assignment to any other duty outside of the VJ which remains within the sole remit of the army. We go from there, Your Honours, to Article 158, which is on page 39 of the English, and I expect the next page in the B/C/S. Now, under Article 158, the ability of the MOD to regulate status or make decisions relating to the service of officers outside the army as claimed by my learned friends is specifically limited to those who have been assigned to the Federal Ministry of Defence. "Authorisation from Article 152 of this law to decide on service relations of professional soldiers and civilian personnel assigned to the Federal Ministry of Defence, shall be carried out by the Federal Minister of Defence." That is the limit of the federal minister of defence's ability to decide on the service of anyone serving outside the VJ. VJ officers serving in the Federal Ministry of Defence only. If we move, Your Honours, to Article 53. And, Mr. Registrar, that's on page 13 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S. Now, this provision, Your Honours, establishes that, to all intents and purposes, there is little difference, none, between an officer, a VJ officer serving in the VJ, and a VJ officer serving outside the VJ. Article 53, the second paragraph: "A professional officer or non-commissioned officer assigned outside the army shall have the same rights and duties of professional officers and non-commissioned officers assigned to the army, unless otherwise stipulated by this law." And there is no such otherwise stipulate. So VJ officers serving outside the army have the same rights and duties as VJ officers serving in a VJ duty or post. Well, what happens if a VJ officer serving outside the army commits a disciplinary infraction or offence? For that, Your Honours, we go to Article 159. It's page 39. Thank you, Mr. Registrar, you are way ahead of me. Right. "A service member who violates military discipline in the performance of his service or in connection with the performance of his service shall be held responsible for disciplinary infractions or disciplinary offences." There is no distinction drawn in this provision between an officer serving in the VJ, a VJ officer serving in the VJ or a VJ officer serving outside the VJ. Under Article 8 service in the VJ includes both. So a service member under Article 9 -- under Article 159 is a service member as defined by Article 8 which includes VJ officers serving in VJ posts and VJ officers serving outside the VJ. All right. So once a VJ officer serving outside the VJ commits an offence for which he is liability under VJ law, who has the responsibility of disciplining? Is it the Ministry of Defence or is it somebody else? And for that, Your Honours, we go to Article 181, which states: "The following individuals are authorised to bring the perpetrator of a disciplinary offence before a military disciplinary court: In the Federal Ministry of Defence," so that's limited to the Federal Ministry of Defence, "the federal minister of defence and commanding officers of the units directly subordinated to him." The only other alternative in the army, that is the VJ, army commander, or senior officer holding an equal or higher position. So, Your Honours, there is no room, there is simply no room to interpret the Law on the VJ as saying, as my learned friend does, that somehow if you are assigned to a post outside of the VJ, that there is no longer authority over that person, disciplinary responsibility over that person, or that you are outside the VJ chain of command. Unless Your Honours have any questions for me, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thomas. Mr. Lukic, any rejoinder? I beg your pardon, I'm sorry, Mr. Lukic, my apologies. Mr. Harmon, I apologise to you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour, I accept them. Thank you. Your Honour, first of all, let me comment on Mr. Lukic's correct assertion that Prosecution Exhibit 2710 is quoted out of context in paragraph 785 of our brief. I do accept that. I apologise for that, but I also note, Your Honours, that the Prosecution Exhibit 2710 is quoted in, and the relevant portions of it are quoted in paragraph 78 and they are quoted in the proper context in that. Now, let me also address a point that Mr. Lukic made this morning, and that is, as you recall, the beginning of my opening remarks, I informed the Trial Chamber that we would not proceed further under Article 7(3) failure to prevent in respect of the counts in Zagreb. The Defence this morning has submitted that this action by the Prosecutor undercuts our assertion that Perisic had effective control over General Celeketic and others. The Prosecution's proper exercise of discretion and discharge of his responsibilities does no such thing. And I would ask you when you consider, first of all, the facts relating to the events in Zagreb, and I need to go into private session for just a minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to address Defence submissions that were made at page 14807 and 14808. Those submissions that the Defence made were as follows: That General Perisic attempted to persuade members of the SDC that people who came from Bosnia and from Croatia who did not want to fight for their homeland had no place in the VJ. Mr. Lukic says that General Perisic could not persuade members of the SDC to accept such a firm position and when General Perisic's proposal was rejected by the SDC, the Defence asserted the following: "General Perisic lost his position of authority which would enable him to order something to anyone to do anything." Next: "He lost his power to issue an order from his position of superior to send anyone to the VRS." And lastly: "His order, therefore, did not have a binding nature, a binding character." Now, I'd like to explore the facts. Your Honours have received Prosecution Exhibit 709 which is the transcript of the 14th session of the SDC and in the English version of that, Your Honour, I'm referring to pages 32 to 36 of that, the context is this: General Perisic had submitted to the SDC a document in which he proposed to the SDC that people who did not want to serve in Croatia or in Bosnia should be expelled from the army if they refused. Now, we submit, Your Honour, and in fact, Mr. Bulatovic who was a member of the SDC agreed with General Perisic. He did, in fact, persuade the SDC of the position he was advocating. They just didn't want the sanctions to be imposed on people who refused to go to the other armies to be so direct. They wanted to indirectly sanction people for their refusals. As Mr. Bulatovic said in this text, he says that it was in the vital interests of the state not to elevate this. He said, he discussed the document that General Perisic had submitted to the SDC and he said, "If this document were to fall in anybody's hands, it would keep us under sanctions for ten years." Mr. Bulatovic said, as a member of the SDC, "I am in favour of applying certain restrictive measures to those who fail to respond to a call-up to defend their people, but not in such a direct manner." General Perisic responded on page 35 of the transcript that he had found a way to solve the problem. I will read General Perisic's solution to the problem of what to do with people who refused orders to go to the VRS or the SVK. And this is at page 35: "I have already issued an internal order that they are all supposed to go there; whoever doesn't want to go has to find a mode; we, too, have found the appropriate criteria. For instance, if someone doesn't want to go and has over 30 years of pensionable employment, we can give him early retirement so that we are not accepting this. We will tell him that he is not performing his duties in a satisfactory manner and other things, but we won't write down that he did not want to go there. So we won't give them any kind of legal stronghold. However, we can rework this order," this is the document that I say parenthetically, this is the document that he had presented to the SDC for its consideration, "however, we can rework this order in all its other segments and submit it to the president, and just leave out the part related to their having to go. We'll find another way of getting rid of them." Now, both the SDC, as I say, and General Perisic agreed that people who didn't want to go should be out of the army. It's just the way in which that would be -- that problem would be resolved. Now, Your Honour, contrary to the Defence assertion, General Perisic did not lose his position of authority as a superior to send someone to the VRS or to the SVK. That's simply not correct. He did send people to the VRS and the SVK. That is in our brief, and I made some submissions on that in my earlier remarks, where there are orders to transfer. We saw an order to transfer people from the various personnel centres back and forth. But he in fact did and he persisted in doing that throughout the war to the end of the war. So he did not lose his authority. Next, contrary to the Defence position that his orders did not have a binding effect, a binding character, it's our submission, first off, that the Law on the Army, P197, Article 37, requires a member of the service to follow an order. If you don't follow an order, Your Honour, it's a disciplinary offence. And according to Mr. Starcevic, a subordinate who received an order was required to obey it. You'll find Mr. Starcevic's testimony at page 5463, lines -- well, 5463, Your Honour. Now, when I say the failure to follow an order was a disciplinary offence, I refer Your Honours to P197, Article 160, subpart (1). It's our submission, contrary to the Defence submission, that none of General Perisic's legal authority was vitiated by the SDC's decision. Let me turn, Your Honour to another aspect of Mr. Lukic's submissions. We had a discussion yesterday and today about context and a large amount of time was the discussion relating to the FRY's desire to have peace at some point in time. And that point in time was when the Contact Group had made a proposal and at that point in time we can see a political divergence between the political leaders of the RS and the political leadership of the FRY. When the RS leaders rejected the Contact Group plan, there was a shift in the attitude of the FRY political leadership. Milosevic was quite upset. The FRY was under sanctions. According to the text we've seen, he wanted the RS leaders to accept the peace plan. Now, his -- as a result of the rejection of the peace plan, the FRY introduced sanctions against the RS. Those sanctions were introduced on the 4th of August, 1994. I have submitted in evidence Prosecution Exhibit 222, Your Honour, and let me tell you what 222 is. It is report. It is an article from a newspaper reporting on the Drina River border being closed and reports on the sanctions. And what it says is, and I'll read this: "The Republika Srpska leadership by rejecting peace has committed the worst act against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Serbian and Montenegrin people, and all other citizens living in these territories. Therefore, the federal government has decided to: Cut political and economic ties with the Republika Srpska; ban Republika Srpska top officials (Assembly, Presidency, government) from FRY territory; the FRY border is closed for all shipments into Republika Srpska except food, clothes, and medicine." Now, Your Honour, this political set of factors that have been described by Mr. Lukic and which resulted in the sanction are quite interesting, but have little bearing on General Perisic's responsibility under Article 7(1) for aiding and abetting by providing men and materiel to the forces in the VRS. I say that, Your Honour, because General Perisic's assistance never did change in respect of the assistance he rendered to the VRS. The FRY border was closed. The assistance continued. We've briefed that point in our final brief. You can find that at paragraphs 283 to 286. The FRY continued to support the VRS with a brief exception, that exception being that they stopped the payment of salaries for a period of five months to the VRS, while at the same time they continued to provide some support to the families of those VRS personnel who were serving -- or those VJ personnel who were serving in the Republika Srpska. At the same time, Your Honour, when the FRY salaries had been cut off, P851 shows that General Perisic sent General Mladic 500.000 dinars to assist in the payment of salaries. Now, we also had, Your Honour, a reference today to a meeting that took place in August of 1995. That meeting was a meeting where a decision was to be taken as to who would represent the Serb interest at Dayton. Milosevic was there, General Perisic was there, General Mladic was there, political leaders from the RS were there. And so was a Serb Orthodox Bishop by the name of Bishop Irinej [phoen], and at some point in the text of those meetings which you have at Prosecution Exhibit 230 and at page 11, Bishop Irinej advocated to President Milosevic the lifting of the Drina River blockade. This is in August of 1995. President Milosevic responded to the Bishop. He said, "the blockade was merely a formality and that aid flows daily." Now, Your Honour, I also refer Your Honours to the testimony of a witness. The transcript reference is 3.522 to 3.525, a discussion about the assistance to the RS, to the VRS. Not only was logistical supplies continued to be directed toward the VRS by General Perisic, but he also continued to send personnel to the VRS. And in that respect, Your Honour, I refer Your Honours to two documents that we have presented. One is Prosecution Exhibit 2519. It's referred to in our -- it refers to an individual by the name of Jankovic. He is discussed in our brief at paragraphs 546 and 547. Let me tell you about P2519. This is a letter that was written by General Mladic to the VJ General Staff and to Perisic requesting specifically that Jankovic be sent to the VRS, a specific request for Jankovic. Jankovic at the time was serving in the VJ General Staff 2nd administration. This request was made months before the events in Srebrenica and you will recall Mr. Jankovic. Mr. Jankovic, if you recall the meetings at the Hotel Fontana that are in evidence, the meetings -- there were three. In those meetings, Mr. Jankovic is present. Specifically, you will recall the meeting on the night of the 11th of July, 1995, when General Mladic is sitting talking to a Muslim representative and saying to that Muslim representative, The fate of your people depends on your decision. It's a very ominous and chilling and threatening conversation with General Mladic and this Muslim representative. Mr. Jankovic was seated next to General Mladic at that time, taking notes and the like. Now, you'll see also, Your Honour, another document, P2518.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just find out how long are you going to be on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are five minutes -- almost three minutes beyond the break time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will conclude my remark. I'll continue, Your Honour, if you like, I'm at your disposal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have no way of knowing how much longer you are going to be. Finish off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd be glad to, Your Honour. The next document is 2518, it deals with an individual by the name of Kosoric. Colonel Kosoric was also a member of the -- he was a member of the Special Unit Corps which was subordinated to General Perisic. There was request for Mr. Kosoric by General Milovanovic, specifically naming Kosoric to come to the VRS. That was dated the 23rd of May, 1995. About a month before the events, a little bit, five weeks before the events in Srebrenica. And Mr. Kosoric is also identified in our trial brief, as I say, paragraphs 549 to 553. You may recall that Kosoric at the conclusion of the meeting with -- on the morning of the 12th of July in the Hotel Fontana informed various people that the inhabitants of Srebrenica were going to be separated, the men were going to be separated and they were going to be executed. Now, I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did he tell them then that that they were going to be executed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, he said they were going to be killed. It's in our brief, Your Honour. I can't tell you the specific paragraph, somewhere between paragraph 549 and 553, you should find that reference. In any event, Your Honour, I think the context that we've heard, Your Honour, from the Defence about Mr. Milosevic wanting peace, asserting peace has little bearing on the 7(1) case that we have against General Perisic. It's our submission, Your Honour, that General Perisic continued to assist the VRS supplying both military materiel and personnel, notwithstanding the political differences between Milosevic and Karadzic and Krajisnik and the like. That, Your Honour, concludes my remarks. I have nothing further to submit, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, we'll then take a break and come back at half past. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will have several comments to make on the submissions we've just heard from our learned friends with regard to the final submissions, the closing arguments of the Defence. I would first like to express a position ever of the Defence that Ms. McKenna referred to, namely, whether the structure and the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia had anything to do with the assistance provided and the provision of the officers corps which in their view has to do with effective control and Article 7(3) with regard to Mr. Perisic's responsibility. We don't share the few of the Prosecution at all. We think that the Prosecution may have neglected the indictment itself because there in paragraphs 29, 30, and 31, where an aspect of aiding and abetting is referred to on the part of the Army of Republika Srpska, and considers all the individuals mentioned in these paragraphs as subordinates of General Perisic and explain the underlying position supporting his command responsibility in relation to them, in that context, what we said about the membership of the army and the superior-subordinate relationship and whether anyone was within or without the VJ, all of this is relevant to establish responsibility under 7(1), if for nothing else then for their allegation of atmosphere of impunity. Now, let me address what Mr. Thomas had to say in relation to my yesterday's words, namely the provisions of the army -- of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, I referred to those provisions as did he, and you yourselves, Your Honours, will have to examine them in your assessment of the evidence. The Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, as all of us here in the courtroom are well aware and as Mr. Thomas mentioned a moment ago, does not provide for the possibility of dispatching VJ personnel to a different country. This was something that Witness Starcevic testified about and it is something you heard the positions of both parties on. You also heard the words of General Perisic at a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council when he discussed the possibilities under the law at a time he was within the Army of Yugoslavia. The Law on the Army of Yugoslavia regulates something else that I discussed, as well as what Mr. Thomas mentioned, and I agree with. An officer of the Army of Yugoslavia, and please look at Article 7, which provides for the composition of the Army of Yugoslavia, who it is who makes up the Army of Yugoslavia. Now, I'm referring to the law. Under that law, an officer of the VJ can be assigned within the Army of Yugoslavia and outside it. The provision of the law that both I and Mr. Thomas referred to deal with the status rights and obligations of the VJ officer who is within the VJ and outside it. The law is quite precise in relation to the Ministry of Defence and in relation to what I invoked, the regulation of the various aspects of the service, appointment, promotion, and termination of service, this has been stipulated very specifically in relation to the Ministry of Defence, because there is a certain hierarchy within the Ministry of Defence. We heard Witnesses Nikolic and Starcevic on this issue. For this reason, the Law on the Army which regulates the status of the VJ personnel within the MOD is very specific. An officer of the VJ, such as Starcevic and Nikolic who were seconded to the MOD, they were, as such, outside of the chain of command of the VJ and within the hierarchy of the MOD. However, their service and their status within that service is regulated as if they were members of the VJ. When an officer of the VJ is, for instance, assigned to a special-purpose industry, he will not be taken out of the VJ chain of command, simply because special-purpose industry doesn't have its own chain of command. That's what the law states and that's why -- that's why they don't have specific provisions referring to them as the MOD does in Articles 151, 158, and 181, so we have a situation whereby the law does not provide for the possibility of a foreign officer to join a different army and we have the status being brought in line with that of the Ministry of Defence and which is specifically envisaged under the law. This particular situation could not have been envisaged by the law, simply because the law does not stipulate that personnel can join an army in a different country. Simply, such a scenario was not envisioned. This was the reason why fictitious virtual documents had to be drawn up on appointments to a different army, something that does not exist in essence, but as we were submitting, they are leaving the chain of command of the VJ simply because they've entered the chain of command of a different army, and simply because you cannot have two chains of command functioning. At transcript page 10532, Witness Starcevic spoke about what the actual state of affairs was given that the law itself did not envisage the possibility for someone to join the ranks of a different army. All of the submissions we made in relation to the provisions of the law indicated how someone in relation to the MOD when it came to appointment, transfers, termination of service and promotions and specifically disciplining, all of this is outside of the VJ, when the individual is within the Ministry of Defence. Including disciplining. Let's make it simple. For instance, I, as a VJ officer, joined the Ministry of Defence where I committed a breach of discipline. It is only within the authority of the minister of defence to initiate disciplinary proceedings against me under the law, and not General Perisic or anyone else from the army. Once I returned to the ranks of the Army of Yugoslavia when I'm assigned to a specific duty, from that point on, General Perisic, or the individuals as regulated by the army service rules, have the authority to initiate disciplinary proceedings or whatever actions against me. This is the submission by the Defence, you have the OTP position with relation to law, and they know themselves because we've been dealing with these facts for the past two years that this is something that was not envisaged by the law. I will not be invoking all the other provisions of the law. I will merely say that this is our interpretation of the law. Mr. Thomas presented us with their interpretation of the law. The two parties, however, do agree on one score on that's that, under the law, it was not envisaged that a VJ officer may be assigned to a different army. What the OTP did not mention, and this is something that we've been discussing for the past two days, first, in relation to aiding and abetting by the provision of the officers corps, and through active actions by General Perisic, i.e., the setting up of the personnel centres, this particular officers corps was given vitality, which enabled them to exist as such, we challenged these OTP submissions, but received no response whatsoever. Your Honours, the army is not an ambivalent, disorganised mass. Every army is a structured organisation which has particular posts occupied by certain individuals. This is what makes up the chain of command and that's how the army works. It is our submission that these individuals whilst they were within the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres, and via those in the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Serbian Krajina were not within the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia, and I will not dwell on this point any longer. There is one other topic I'd like to address. I'd like to make two brief comments and then I'll finish and they have to do with what Mr. Harmon mentioned a moment ago. They have to do with the sanctions imposed by the FRY after the rejection of the Contact Group Plan. I think that the rebuttal in this sense went beyond the scope of our discussions, but still I have to address the comments he made to the effect that the sanctions imposed by General Perisic were not honoured. First off, what we mentioned, above all, in relation to political leaderships and the relationship between the Army of Yugoslavia and leadership of the VRS and SVK, is something that we presented in relation to influence and control, in relation to the existence or non-existence of a superior-subordinate relationship, which you need to establish in order to establish command responsibility. The Defence never contested, and we even invoke these documents, this was earlier on in private sessions, we are in public session now, but we can say that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, despite the fact that it introduced sanctions upon Republika Srpska in August of 1994, a certain while later resumed the provision of assistance to both the VRS and the SVK, as well as to both these countries, the RS and the RSK. I'll remind you that we showed these Supreme Defence Council's decisions from May and June of 1995 to witnesses and especially after Storm when it was said quite decidedly that assistance to the RS would continue, in view of the general situation which posed a threat to the stability of the FRY, insofar as it may pose a threat to its combat readiness. That's what the decision said. And we take no issue with the statement by Milosevic which Mr. Harmon referred to this that this assistance was continued. We submit that it did not continue throughout the existence of the sanctions, that the Army of Yugoslavia consistently enforced these sanctions insofar as it concerned the powers of the VJ until such time as the SDS ordered that assistance should be provided again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we wanted to correct that part of the transcript. Page 65, line 25, I said Supreme Defence Council. SDC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: SDC. Okay. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that I've stopped, let me make a small correction. Page 63, line 4, I said Witness Nikolic, not Witness Starcevic at that point. Mr. Harmon mentioned the Exhibit which had to do with the loan of 500.000 dinars that General Perisic gave to General Mladic. Those were two documents. One was Perisic's and the other was Mladic's letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think Mr. Harmon characterised it as a loan. I do not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Bear with me, please. Then I misinterpreted him. I use the term "loan" because that was how the amount was characterised in one of these two documents, so my apologies to Mr. Harmon, but that was also the testimony of Witness Petrovic, and as you will see one of the two documents used the term "loan". Bear with me for a moment, Your Honours. To avoid any confusion with regard to the Defence's position on this issue, and in paragraph 365 of our final trial brief in relation to the loan of 500.000 dinars, we expressed what our view was in relation to the loan. We assert that, at the time, the Defence minister Pavle Bulatovic was privy to that loan and even discussed it, you have it in footnote 658 of our trial brief, where we referred to one of his statements in the minutes, 572 page 89, that's minutes of the Supreme Defence Council. Thank you, Your Honours. If you have any questions, I'm prepared to answer them. But these were the comments that we wished to make in relation to the Prosecutor's rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. It remains for the Chamber just to thank the parties for the conduct of the trial from the beginning to now. We've now reached the end, almost, and pursuant to Rule 87A, of the Rules of Procedure, the Chamber declares the hearing closed and the Chamber will retreat to go and deliberate, and the parties will hear judgement on a date to be determined. Court adjourned.
